summary: A short poster paper with 2,700 prompt pairs: 3 risk scenarios (ambiguous requirements, under-specified operational context, security-functionality conflict) x 9 languages x 50 pairs. Prompts come from GitHub issues, Stack Overflow, 'anonymized internal developer logs' and hand-written CWE-guided prompts. Each risk-inducing prompt is paired with a version that adds security guidance or rewrites the request. Outputs from 8 LLMs (5 samples at T=1) are labeled secure/vulnerable using CodeQL/Clang plus GPT-5-assisted 'expert review'. It reports baseline vulnerability above 56% for every model (66% for ambiguous requirements) and 37-45% reductions with security-aware prompts, with regressions up to 19% in the conflict scenario. Results appear only in figures, and the dataset is unreleased.

claims.claim: All eight models have average vulnerability rates above 56% under realistic risk scenarios
claims.evidence: Fig. 3(a), figure only. Labels come from static analyzers plus GPT-5-assisted expert review. The number of experts, sampling, agreement and per-language coverage are unreported (CodeQL/Clang cover Bash, HTML and SQL poorly). Expert review of ~216k outputs (2,700 x 2 rounds x 5 samples x 8 models) is not plausible without a sampling protocol, and none is described.

claims.claim: Security-aware prompting improves security by up to 45%
claims.evidence: §3.3: Claude-Sonnet-4 shows a 'vulnerability-rate reduction of up to 45%' and Qwen3-4B 37%; it is unclear whether these are absolute pp or relative. The treatment adds the missing security requirements (and for SC3 reformulates the request), so this compares an under-specified prompt with a specified one, not a mitigation technique with an alternative.

claims.claim: Ambiguous requirements are the riskiest scenario (66%) and security-functionality conflict the lowest (52%)
Security prompting regresses in conflict scenarios (regression up to 19%, net gain 0.12)
claims.evidence: Text in §3.3; figure-only support, same labeling caveats.

patterns.note: Making security requirements explicit in the prompt lowers vulnerability rates for all 8 models, but regresses up to 19% when the request conflicts with security. Paired within-prompt design, figure-only numbers, unvalidated labels. No comparison against analyzer-in-the-loop or agent scaffolds.
The ambiguous-requirement scenario (66% vulnerable) motivates eliciting security requirements before generation; asking is never tested.
CodeQL and Clang Static Analyzer are used only as labeling aids, not as feedback in the generation loop.

methodology.sample: 2,700 prompt pairs (50 per scenario x language); 5 samples per prompt per model
methodology.baselines: Risk-inducing vs security-augmented prompt (within-pair); no scaffold, agent or analyzer-feedback condition
methodology.models: Qwen3-Max, Claude-Sonnet-4, DeepSeek-V3-0324, GPT-5, Grok-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-4B, GLM-Z1-Air
methodology.variance: 5 samples at T=1.0 but no intervals or tests reported
methodology.contamination_controls: None; prompts are partly drawn from public GitHub and Stack Overflow
methodology.languages: Bash, HTML, JavaScript, C++, Java, PHP, Go, SQL, Python

standards.peer_review: Poster; venue not stated in arXiv metadata
standards.artifacts: None; dataset 'will be released upon publication'

biases.detail: GPT-5-assisted labeling with an undescribed expert-review protocol and no agreement statistics.
The 'mitigation' supplies the missing requirement or rewrites the task, so the improvement measures specification completeness rather than a prompting technique.
Benchmark and labels unreleased; 'internal developer logs' of unstated provenance.

verdict_reason: On-topic and broad (8 models, 9 languages, paired prompts), and the direction agrees with prior work that under-specified prompts yield insecure code. But it is a poster with figure-only results, an opaque and implausible-at-scale labeling protocol, no released data, and a 'mitigation' that is really a fuller specification. Use only as weak corroboration.
applicability: For pre-spec work: when requirements are ambiguous, models do not default to secure code (66% vulnerable in that scenario). The team's spec template or clarification checklist should therefore elicit security and operational-context requirements explicitly (authentication, PHI/PII handling for healthcare-education content, public vs internal exposure, Spring Boot/Spring Security versions) before generation. Enforce them with deterministic checks (Semgrep/Sonar rules already in qr), not prompt text alone. The poster's own conflict-scenario regressions, and 2606.25195's finding that scaffolds and executable feedback beat security prompting, both argue against relying on prompts.

conflicts_with.detail: Finds executable feedback and agent scaffolding give larger secure-code gains than security prompting. This poster presents security-aware prompting as the mitigation without comparing it with scaffolds or analyzer-in-the-loop.
